title: You’re Thinking About Online Trends All Wrong
gist: NYU cyber-ethnographer Ruby Thelot argues virality has collapsed as a cultural indicator under Goodhart's law — it can now be engineered without ever trickling down to culture — because the internet has balkanized into 'digital islands.' He backs this with his own sample of ~1,000 Instagram and TikTok videos over 1M views showing only ~25% negative sentiment on dating, reframes Kalshi/Polymarket betting as a participation ritual rather than a financial instrument, and argues AI doom is misconceived because the world's problems are bottlenecked by coordination, not intelligence.

insights.claim: Virality has become a target rather than a proxy, so under Goodhart's law it has ceased to be a valid measure of cultural adoption — content can be engineered to enormous view counts without ever acquiring cultural staying power.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: Any consumer or media thesis underwritten by view counts and engagement metrics is measuring the optimization target, not demand — discount view-based TAM estimates accordingly.
insights.quote: Because we are so far into Goodhart’s law in terms of culture, you can engineer virality without it ever trickling down to culture.
insights.locator: The problem with our attempt to understand culture

insights.claim: The internet has balkanized into 'digital islands' where most apparently viral phenomena are the product of force-fed algorithmic consumption, so virality now exists between provinces rather than among the masses.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: Trend-spotting that reads a single feed as a mass signal will systematically overestimate addressable audience; segment-level penetration is the number that matters.
insights.quote: This is where virality primarily exists today: between provinces, not among the masses.
insights.locator: Thelot, a cyber-ethnographer and media theory researcher at NYU

insights.claim: Recent hype cycles that failed to convert into durable behavior — NFTs and audio-chat apps like Clubhouse pitched as the future of social media — demonstrate that even specialist tech press repeatedly mistakes short-term engagement for long-term adoption.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: A base rate worth pricing: platform-format hype has a poor conversion record, and the outlets amplifying it have no better hit rate than the market.
insights.quote: Or that period when audio chat apps like Clubhouse were pitched as the future of social media but quickly flamed out? (A prediction WIRED was not immune to.)
insights.locator: While trends like “6-7” and “looksmaxxing” have recently broken containment

themes.theme: The dating-burnout narrative fails its own data

insights.claim: A sample of roughly 1,000 Instagram and TikTok videos with over 1 million views each found that only about 25 percent of dating-related content was actually negative, undercutting the widely reported 'heteropessimism' malaise narrative.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: Product pivots justified by a 'burnout' narrative may be solving for a sentiment that exists in commentary more than in user behavior — a fundamental risk to dating-app repositioning bets.
insights.locator: We wanted to know: What is the percentage of things that are actually negative?

insights.claim: Dating burnout discourse has already driven product decisions — Bumble announced in May that it was killing its swipe feature to lure users back, and the category has rebranded around AI.
insights.speaker: Jason Parham
insights.so_what: A core-mechanic removal is a high-variance retention bet; watch whether Bumble's engagement recovers or whether the burnout premise was mostly a media artifact.
insights.locator: Dating burnout has gotten a lot of attention

insights.claim: Negativity levels differ by platform because algorithms differ — X is characterized as having a trickier algorithm that surfaces more negative content — so cross-platform sentiment readings measure the recommender as much as the population.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: Sentiment scraped from one platform is not a population estimate; brand and consumer research sourced from a single feed carries an embedded algorithmic bias.
insights.locator: And I wanted to compare—is there one platform that is more negative

themes.theme: Prediction markets as participation, not finance

insights.claim: Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket should be modeled not merely as financial instruments but as tools for participation, because consumers no longer want to purely consume culture — they want to buy into it.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: If engagement rather than expected value drives volume, prediction-market growth is less rate-sensitive and less edge-sensitive than a trading business — it behaves like entertainment ARPU.
insights.quote: With prediction markets, I think about them not merely as financial instruments, but also as a tool for participation.
insights.locator: When I think about the male loneliness epidemic

insights.claim: For heavy users the financial reward is not the driver of wagering — after eight hours on screen the operative question is 'How do I get closer to it?', and the bet itself is largely irrelevant except as the mechanism of closeness to media.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: A user base betting for proximity rather than profit is far more tolerant of negative expected value, which supports durable take rates but invites the consumer-protection scrutiny that follows gambling.
insights.quote: If you're spending eight hours on the screen, the question is not “How do I make money with this?” It is “How do I get closer to it?” The bet, for the most part, does not matter.
insights.locator: But I don't even think that the financial award is what is driving people to gamble

insights.claim: Meme coin trading among young men from 2020 to 2024 was primarily a social rather than individual activity, conducted in group chats called 'the trenches' where participants exchanged information, traded together, and lost together — a novel form of male bonding that prediction markets now inherit.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: Retail speculation with a social-bonding function is stickier than pure P&L-driven activity; churn models built on returns alone will underestimate retention.
insights.quote: It tended to be in these group chats, lovingly called “the trenches,” in which you and your boys exchanged information and traded together. And not only that, you lose together.
insights.locator: I spent some time studying groups of young men who were trading meme coins

insights.claim: AI will not end the world because most global problems are not bottlenecked by intelligence but by cooperation, coordination, and alignment of large groups of people toward a shared goal.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: If the binding constraint is coordination rather than cognition, the returns to raw model capability plateau earlier than compute-scaling narratives assume.
insights.quote: I don’t think AI is going to end the world. And the reason is that I don't think intelligence is that important.
insights.locator: AI is reshaping culture at light speed

insights.claim: The belief that intelligence is the most powerful force traces to the same assumption held by Sir Francis Galton, the father of eugenics — that a most-intelligent group of people exists — meaning superintelligence advocates are projecting what they value about themselves onto the technology.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: The intellectual lineage argument is becoming a mainstream line of attack on AGI discourse — a reputational and regulatory vector for labs whose pitch rests on superintelligence framing.
insights.quote: With AI, they are just projecting what they value about themselves onto the superintelligence. It’s philosophically unsound and actually quite dangerous.
insights.locator: The belief that intelligence is the most powerful thing

insights.claim: Quantifying intelligence forecloses untapped human capacities — emotional, bodily, and artistic intelligence — because, following Gilbert Simondon, each technical advance leaves certain things behind that current systems do not measure.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: Categories of value that benchmarks cannot score are where non-AI-substitutable services and products will retain pricing power.
insights.quote: In that process, you're foreclosing a whole slew of untapped values—emotional intelligence, bodily intelligence, artistic intelligence.

insights.claim: Goodhart's law recurs as a second failure mode inside AI itself: once a capability is quantified, the metric becomes the goal in and of itself, repeating the same measurement collapse that destroyed virality as a cultural signal.
insights.speaker: Ruby Thelot
insights.so_what: Benchmark scores are the AI equivalent of view counts — expect the same divergence between measured capability and delivered value.
insights.quote: The second thing is, when you start to quantify specific things, once again, the metric becomes the goal in and of itself.
insights.locator: Most of our issues in the world are not bottlenecked by intelligence
